Conflict demography faces a data paradox. The populations most affected by civil conflict tend to have the weakest vital registration systems, the least reliable cause-of-death coding, and the most disrupted statistical infrastructure. Methods that rely on detailed conflict event databases, ICD-coded mortality records, or large-scale retrospective household surveys are most needed precisely where they are least feasible. Meanwhile, the demographic data sources with the highest quality and longest coverage — such as the Human Mortality Database — are dominated by stable, affluent nations that have largely been spared the worst forms of internal conflict [@hmd2024].

This paper proposes a comparatively lightweight approach. We argue that intense civil conflicts with sectarian or tit-for-tat dynamics produce a characteristic signature in all-cause mortality surfaces: an impulse-decay pattern in which excess mortality, concentrated in young adult males, rises sharply at the onset of conflict and then decays exponentially over years or decades. This signature can be detected and quantified using only all-cause mortality data disaggregated by age, sex, and calendar year — without cause-of-death coding, conflict event databases, or retrospective attribution.

The approach builds on the insight of @girosiking2008 that mortality surfaces are fundamentally smooth spatial objects: mortality at a given age and year is expected to be similar to mortality at neighbouring ages and years. Smooth priors over the Lexis surface encode this expectation. Departures from smoothness therefore carry information. The impulse-decay signature of conflict is precisely such a departure — too abrupt for a smooth prior to absorb, yet too structured to dismiss as noise. It is a parametric anomaly with a specific, interpretable shape.

We develop a Bayesian framework that jointly estimates (i) a smooth baseline mortality surface and (ii) zero or more impulse-decay conflict components, with the timing of onset, rate of decay, and age-specific magnitude all estimated from the data rather than assumed from historical knowledge. Model comparison provides a principled detection criterion: populations where the impulse-decay model substantially outperforms the smooth baseline are identified as carrying a conflict-attributable mortality signature.

We validate the approach on Northern Ireland, where the Troubles (1968--1998) left a well-documented demographic scar and where direct conflict-death tallies provide ground truth for comparison. We apply it to Algeria, where the "Black Decade" (1991--2002) produced a qualitatively similar but faster-decaying signature. We then conduct a systematic scan of all Human Mortality Database countries to test whether the method detects conflict signatures where expected and does not falsely detect them in stable populations.

The impulse-decay model characterises conflicts along two dimensions: initial intensity and persistence (half-life). These parameters are substantively meaningful. A long half-life (as in Northern Ireland, ~7 years) suggests entrenched, self-sustaining tit-for-tat dynamics; a shorter half-life (as in Algeria, ~3 years) suggests a more acute phase that burns out faster. The model also challenges dominant narratives about peace processes, suggesting — at least in the Northern Irish case — that key political events on the road to peace followed rather than led the underlying decline in violence.

The paper proceeds as follows. @sec-history provides historical context for the Northern Irish case. @sec-methods introduces the impulse-decay model, the Bayesian estimation framework, and the systematic scan protocol. @sec-results presents results for Northern Ireland, Algeria, and the HMD-wide scan. @sec-discussion compares our estimates with existing conflict-death tallies, discusses what decay rates reveal about conflict dynamics, and considers the method's applicability to data-sparse settings beyond the HMD.
